name: Broadway Triangle
headline: Piecemeal housing buildout
why: A 30-acre pocket bounded by Broadway, Flushing Ave and Union Ave, former Pfizer land plus city-owned lots, long stalled after its rezoning was challenged as discriminatory.
history: Pfizer opened here in 1849 and by the early 1900s occupied the full block now called Broadway Triangle. Manufacturing ran until 2008, after its HQ moved to Manhattan in 1961. Earlier use is unknown.
now: Rabsky Group's eight-building, 1,146-apartment project on the former Pfizer blocks keeps opening in phases; 25% of units are affordable. A lottery for 120 affordable units at 11 Gerry St ran through March 2026.
owner: Rabsky Group owns the rezoned parcels. Some adjacent lots remain city-owned.

name: Greenpoint Hospital Campus
headline: Affordable homes rising, seniors wait
neighborhood: 288 Jackson St · Bed-Stuy / East Williamsburg border
why: The former Greenpoint Hospital campus, closed in 1982, is being rebuilt as Kingsland Commons: about 557 affordable homes, senior housing and a 200-bed shelter across four phases.
history: Before the hospital, this was Peter Cooper's glue factory (c. 1845-1915), one of the city's largest. The hospital opened October 4, 1915, run by the city, and closed in December 1982 after 70 years.
now: The shelter phase opened in 2025 and the 311-unit second phase is nearly done, with its lottery due soon. A temporary city shelter placed on site in March 2026 is delaying the senior housing phase; neighbors rallied Sept 17.
owner: NYC (HPD) owns the site. Hudson Companies and St. Nicks Alliance are developing it; Project Renewal runs the shelter.

name: Monitor Point
headline: Approved 1,324-unit housing
neighborhood: 40-56 Quay St · Greenpoint waterfront, by Bushwick Inlet Park
why: A low-rise MTA auto-repair yard at 40 Quay St and the Greenpoint Monitor Museum's empty lot beside Bushwick Inlet, land many locals wanted added to the park promised in 2005.
history: 56 Quay St was Motiva land, donated in 2003 to found the Greenpoint Monitor Museum, honoring the nearby shipyard that built the ironclad USS Monitor in 1862. 40 Quay St was an MTA auto-repair yard.
now: The full City Council approved the rezoning on July 16, 2026 after Council Member Restler won more affordability: 662 of at least 1,324 apartments will be affordable, in towers of 56, 41 and 35 stories on land leased from the MTA.
owner: MTA owns the land. Gotham Organization is the developer.

name: River Ring
headline: Tax break secured, towers years off
neighborhood: River St between N 1st and N 3rd Sts · Williamsburg waterfront
why: Parking and empty lots on the former Con Edison fuel-oil terminal, where Two Trees plans two towers, a YMCA, a public beach and a waterfront park.
history: This was Con Edison's North First St fuel-oil terminal. Two Trees bought it in 2019 for $150M and later removed the tanks, though caissons and bulkhead remnants remain. Earlier use is unconfirmed.
now: In May 2026 the state budget extended the old 421a tax break for River Ring past its 2031 deadline. Two Trees says the first of two towers (710 and 560 ft, about 1,200 apartments, 30% affordable) likely won't finish until 2033.

headline: Three towers planned
neighborhood: 21 & 37 Freeman St, 209 West St · Greenpoint waterfront, north of Transmitter Park
why: Vacant waterfront lots on Freeman St, Block C of Greenpoint Landing, the 22-acre, 5,500-apartment master plan that grew out of the 2005 rezoning.
history: This waterfront corridor held some of the 50+ oil refineries that operated 1860s-1960s. WNYC's transmitter ran just south of here 1937-1990. No source ties a specific occupant to this parcel.
now: Domain, LMXD and Park Tower Group plan three towers of 40, 30 and 9 stories with about 1,025 apartments, 300 affordable. They closed $114 million in land financing in Aug 2025 and expected to start building in summer 2026.

name: Transmitter Park
headline: Marina plan scrapped
why: An NYC Parks waterfront park, opened in 2012 on the former WNYC radio transmitter site, where a proposed restaurant and marina drew strong neighborhood opposition.
history: This spot was Greenpoint's ferry terminal 1853-1933. The city set it aside for WNYC in 1935. The WPA-funded transmitter building was dedicated in 1937 and broadcast until 1990.
now: On Sept 15, 2026, NYC Parks dropped the restaurant and 40-slip marina at a Community Board 1 committee meeting. A proposed resolution seeks a restroom concession and swaps the 1937 building's required renovation for a plaque.

name: Bushwick Inlet Park
headline: Parkland still undelivered
why: Promised as parkland in the city's 2005 rezoning in exchange for upzoning, large sections of the planned park remain undelivered more than 20 years later.
history: The largest undelivered section sits on the former Astral Oil Works (later Standard Oil, sold in the 1940s), then the Bayside Fuel Oil Depot until it closed in 2010. Tanks came down in 2019.
now: The Motiva section around the inlet opened April 30, 2026, bringing the park to about 9 of 27.8 promised acres. The 8.5-acre CitiStorage parcel is next, but cleanup is slow and Restler says completion is short $75M to $100M.
owner: NYC Parks owns the site. Large sections of the planned park remain undelivered.

name: Grand Army Plaza Redesign
headline: Proposed plaza redesign
why: A landmarked traffic circle and plaza at the entrance to Prospect Park, now the subject of a major reconstruction proposal.
history: Laid out as Olmsted and Vaux's Prospect Park entrance starting in 1866. The Soldiers' and Sailors' Arch went up 1889-92. The current Bailey Fountain dates to 1929-32. Landmarked 1973-75.
now: Mayor Mamdani and DOT proposed closing a roadway in April 2026 to link the arch to Prospect Park. DOT updated five community boards June 2: the plan adds 42% more public space but still needs capital design and landmarks review.
owner: NYC (public right-of-way, under NYC DOT jurisdiction).

name: Park Avenue / BQE Corridor
headline: Corridor concepts under study
neighborhood: 100 Park Ave (representative point) · under the BQE, Fort Greene/Clinton Hill end of the corridor
why: The elevated BQE viaduct and underused street space beneath it along Park Avenue, the subject of a fight over what replaces this aging highway.
history: Before the BQE, this was an at-grade industrial street near the Navy Yard (Rockwood Chocolate, Drake's Cakes). This segment was among the last finished, completed around 1960.
now: NYC DOT's October 2024 BQE North and South report floated long-term concepts for the corridor, including this stretch: street redesigns, bike and bus lanes, new plazas and highway capping.
